title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 153 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 760–766 (Night 153, continuing directly from nights-152), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 153 begins a new tale, set in the reign of Hārūn al-Rashīd. Abū al-Ḥasan ibn Ṭāhir, a rich merchant welcome in the caliph's palace, keeps a shop where a young Persian prince, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, often sits with him. One day a lady riding among ten slave-girls stops at the shop, and ʿAlī is struck to the heart at the sight of her. She sends for the two men, and they are led into the caliph's palace, through hall after hall of singing girls, until she appears: Shams al-Nahār, a favourite of Hārūn al-Rashīd. Song follows song; the two lovers fall fainting into each other's arms, and the night ends over a feast and a cup of wine. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-third night,
sentences.n: al-thālitha, “the third”, is the ordinal, feminine to agree with layla; al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّهُ كَانَ فِي قَدِيمِ الزَّمَانِ وَسَالِفِ الْعَصْرِ وَالْأَ وَانِ فِي خِلَافَةِ الْمَلِكِ هَارُونَ الرَّشِيدِ رَجُلٌ تَاجِرٌ لَهُ وَلَدٌ يُسَمَّى أَبَا الْحَسَنِ عَلِيًّا بْنَ طَاهِرٍ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu annahu kāna fī qadīmi al-zamāni wa-sālifi al-ʿaṣri wa-al-awāni fī khilāfati al-maliki hārūna al-rashīdi rajulun tājirun lahu waladun yusammā abā al-ḥasani ʿaliyyan ibna ṭāhirin
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that there was, in the ancient-part of the time and the bygone-part of the age and the era, in the caliphate of the king Hārūn al-Rashīd, a man, a merchant; to-him a son who was-named Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī son of Ṭāhir.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that long ago, in ages past and times gone by, in the caliphate of King Hārūn al-Rashīd, there was a merchant who had a son named Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Ṭāhir.
sentences.n: A new tale begins here, that of Abū al-Ḥasan, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. fī qadīm al-zamān wa-sālif al-ʿaṣr wa-al-awān, “in the ancient part of time and the bygone part of the age and the era”, is the storyteller's stock opening. The print splits al-awān, “time, era”, across a space (والا وان); the spacing is kept. yusammā, “he is named”, takes the name in the accusative: abā (not abū) al-Ḥasan, ʿaliyyan. ibn standing between two names in apposition is written without its alif (بن).

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلُ كَثِيرَ الْمَالِ غَزِيرَ النَّوَالِ وَكَانَ وَالِهُ حَسَنَ الصُّورَةِ مَحْبُوبَ السِّيرَةِ عِنْدَ جَمِيعِ النَّاسِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika al-rajulu kathīra al-māli ghazīra al-nawāli wa-kāna wālihu ḥasana al-ṣūrati maḥbūba al-sīrati ʿinda jamīʿi al-nāsi
sentences.l: And that man was abundant of the wealth, copious of the bounty; and [his son] was fair of the form, beloved of the conduct, with all the people.
sentences.i: That man had great wealth and gave freely, and [his son] was handsome of face and loved by everyone for his ways.
sentences.n: kathīr al-māl … ghazīr al-nawāl, “much of wealth … copious of bounty”, is a rhymed pair. The print's واله gives no sense here: no word with these letters fits as the subject of kāna. The likeliest intended word is ولده, waladuhu, “his son”, which the story requires, since it is the son who frequents the palace in what follows; but the letters differ by more than a dot and other readings cannot be ruled out, so the print is kept, pointed wālihu only to give the letters a reading, and the translation follows “his son” in brackets.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ يَدْخُلُ دَارَ الْخِلَافَةِ مِنْ غَيْرِ إِذْنٍ وَيُحِبُّهُ جَمِيعُ سَرَارِى الْخَلِيفَةِ وَجَوَارِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna yadkhulu dāra al-khilāfati min ghayri idhnin wa-yuḥibbuhu jamīʿu sarārī al-khalīfati wa-jawārīhi
sentences.l: And he used-to enter the house of the caliphate without permission, and there loved-him all the concubines of the caliph and his slave-girls.
sentences.i: He would enter the caliph's palace without asking leave, and all the caliph's concubines and slave-girls were fond of him.
sentences.n: dār al-khilāfa, “the abode of the caliphate”, the caliph's palace. sarārī, plural of surriyya, “concubine”; the print writes the final yāʾ as ى, as it often does.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ يُنَادِمُ الْمَلِكَ وَيُنْشِدُ لَهُ الْأَشْعَارَ وَيُحَدِّثُهُ بِنَوَادِرِ الْأَخْبَارِ إِلَّا أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَبِيعُ وَيَشْتَرِي فِى سُوقِ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna yunādimu al-malika wa-yunshidu lahu al-ashʿāra wa-yuḥaddithuhu bi-nawādiri al-akhbāri illā annahu kāna yabīʿu wa-yashtarī fī sūqi al-tujjāri
sentences.l: And he used-to be-boon-companion-to the king, and recite to-him the poems, and tell-him of the rarities of the reports; except that he used-to sell and buy in the market of the merchants.
sentences.i: He was the king's boon companion, reciting poems to him and entertaining him with rare and curious stories; and yet he bought and sold in the merchants' market.
sentences.n: nādama, “to be someone's boon companion (nadīm)”, to drink and talk with him. ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell (someone) of”: the verb takes bi- for the thing told. The shadda of الّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ يَجْلِسُ عَلَى دُكَّانِهِ شَابٌّ مِنْ أَوْلَادِ مُلُوكِ الْعَجَمِ يُقَالُ لَهُ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna yajlisu ʿalā dukkānihi shābbun min awlādi mulūki al-ʿajami yuqālu lahu ʿaliyyu ibnu bakkārin
sentences.l: And there used-to sit on his-shop a youth of the sons of the kings of the Persians; it-was-said to-him ʿAlī son of Bakkār.
sentences.i: And at his shop there used to sit a young man, one of the sons of the kings of Persia, called ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.
sentences.n: al-ʿajam, “the non-Arabs”, in the Nights usually the Persians. yuqālu lahu, “it is said to him”, is the usual way of giving a name: “called”. One sat “on” a shop, on the raised bench at its front, hence ʿalā.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الشَّابُّ مَلِيحَ الْقَامَةِ ظَرِيفَ الشَّكْلِ كَامِلَ الصُّورَةِ مُوَرَّدَ الْخَدَّيْنِ مَقْرُونَ الْحَاجِبَيْنِ عَذْبَ الْكَلَامِ ضَاحِكَ السِّنِّ يُحِبُّ الْبَسْطَ وَالِانْشِرَاحَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika al-shābbu malīḥa al-qāmati ẓarīfa al-shakli kāmila al-ṣūrati muwarrada al-khaddayni maqrūna al-ḥājibayni ʿadhba al-kalāmi ḍāḥika al-sinni yuḥibbu al-basṭa wa-al-inshirāḥa
sentences.l: And that youth was comely of the stature, elegant of the shape, perfect of the form, rose-tinted of the two-cheeks, joined of the two-eyebrows, sweet of the speech, laughing of the tooth, loving the merriment and the cheerfulness.
sentences.i: That young man was graceful of figure, elegant in his bearing and perfect of face, with rosy cheeks and eyebrows that met, sweet of speech and quick to smile, and he loved pleasure and good cheer.
sentences.n: A string of construct epithets, “X of the Y”, each an accusative predicate of kāna. maqrūn al-ḥājibayn, “joined of the eyebrows”: brows that meet above the nose, counted a beauty. ḍāḥik al-sinn, “laughing of tooth”, smiling, cheerful. basṭ and inshirāḥ, “expansiveness” and “opening of the breast”, both mean gaiety. The shadda of مورّد is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّهُمَا كَانَا جَالِسَيْنِ يَتَحَدَّثَانِ وَيَضْحَكَانِ وَإِذَا بِعَشْرِ جَوَارٍ كَأَنَّهُنَّ الْأَقْمَارُ وَكُلٌّ مِنْهُنَّ ذَاتُ حُسْنٍ وَجَمَالٍ وَقَدٍّ وَاعْتِدَالٍ
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa annahumā kānā jālisayni yataḥaddathāni wa-yaḍḥakāni wa-idhā bi-ʿashri jawārin ka-annahunna al-aqmāru wa-kullun minhunna dhātu ḥusnin wa-jamālin wa-qaddin wa-iʿtidālin
sentences.l: And it-chanced that the-two were sitting, talking-together and laughing, and behold, ten slave-girls as-though they (were) the moons, and each of-them possessed of beauty and loveliness and stature and symmetry.
sentences.i: It chanced one day, as the two of them sat talking and laughing, that there came ten slave-girls like so many moons, every one of them lovely and fair, tall and finely proportioned.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold!”: idhā of surprise, with bi- only marking what suddenly appears. ʿashr, “ten”, has no tāʾ marbūṭa because the counted noun, jawārin, “slave-girls” (plural of jāriya), is feminine. qadd, “stature”, and iʿtidāl, “symmetry, a well-proportioned figure”, make the second of two rhyming pairs (ḥusn wa-jamāl, qadd wa-iʿtidāl).

sentences.t: وَبَيْنَهُنَّ صَبِيَّةٌ رَاكِبَةٌ عَلَى بَغْلَةٍ بِسَرْجٍ مُزَرْكَشٍ لَهُ رِكَابٌ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَعَلَيْهَا إِزَارٌ رَفِيعٌ وَفِي وَسَطِهَا زُنَّارٌ مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ مُطَرَّزٌ بِالذَّهَبِ وَهِيَ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: wa-baynahunna ṣabiyyatun rākibatun ʿalā baghlatin bi-sarjin muzarkashin lahu rikābun mina al-dhahabi wa-ʿalayhā izārun rafīʿun wa-fī wasaṭihā zunnārun mina al-ḥarīri muṭarrazun bi-al-dhahabi wa-hiya kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And among-them a young-woman riding on a she-mule with a saddle brocaded, to-it stirrups of the gold; and on-her a wrap fine, and in her-middle a girdle of the silk embroidered with the gold; and she (was) as said concerning-her the poet:
sentences.i: Among them was a young woman riding a mule with a brocaded saddle and stirrups of gold. She wore a wrap of fine stuff, and about her waist was a girdle of silk embroidered with gold; she was as the poet has said:
sentences.n: muzarkash, “brocaded, worked with gold thread”, from Persian zar-kash. lahu, “to it”, refers back to the saddle. izār, a large wrap or mantle over the whole body. zunnār, “girdle, belt”, a loanword from Greek.

sentences.t:
لَهَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُ الْحَرِيْرِ وَمَنْطِقٌ * رَخِيْمُ الْحَوَاشِي لَاهُرَاءٌ وَلَا نَذْرُ
وَعَيْنَانِ قَالَ اللّٰهُ كُوْنَا فَكَانَتَا * فَعُوْلَانِ بِالْاَلْبَابِ مَاتَفْعَلُ الْخَمْرُ
فَيَا حُبَّهَا زِدْنِي جَوًى كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ * وَيَا سُلْوَةَ الْاَحْبَابِ مَوْعِدُكَ الْحَشْرُ
sentences.tr:
lahā basharun mithlu al-ḥarīri wa-manṭiqun * rakhīmu al-ḥawāshī lā hurāʾun wa-lā nadhru
wa-ʿaynāni qāla allāhu kūnā fa-kānatā * faʿūlāni bi-al-albābi mā tafʿalu al-khamru
fa-yā ḥubbahā zidnī jawan kulla laylatin * wa-yā sulwata al-aḥbābi mawʿiduka al-ḥashru
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the sukūn on long vowels (الْحَرِيْرِ, كُوْنَا) and the bare alif of الْاَلْبَابِ and الْاَحْبَابِ, where the edition marks no hamza. The print runs لا هراء together (لَاهُرَاءٌ), and ما تفعل (مَاتَفْعَلُ). hurāʾ is wordy, empty talk. The print's نَذْرُ means “vow”, which gives no sense here; it very probably stands for نَزْرُ, nazr, “scanty, too few words”, so that her speech is neither too much nor too little, and it is translated so. kūnā, “be!”, is a dual imperative, addressed to the two eyes. faʿūlān, dual of the intensive pattern faʿūl, “the two that greatly do”: they do to minds what wine does. jawā, the inward burning of love or grief. al-ḥashr, “the Gathering” of the dead at the Resurrection: comfort will not come before then.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلْنَ إِلَى دُكَّانِ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ نَزَلَتْ تِلْكَ الْجَارِيَةُ عَنِ الْبَغْلَةِ وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى دُكَّانِهِ فَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣalna ilā dukkāni abī al-ḥasani nazalat tilka al-jāriyatu ʿani al-baghlati wa-jalasat ʿalā dukkānihi fa-sallamat ʿalayhi wa-sallama ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And when they(f.)-arrived at the shop of Abū al-Ḥasan, that girl got-down from the she-mule and sat on his-shop; and she-greeted him, and he-greeted her.
sentences.i: When they reached Abū al-Ḥasan's shop, the young woman dismounted from the mule and sat down at his shop. She greeted him, and he returned her greeting.
sentences.n: waṣalna, “they arrived”, is the feminine plural: the women of the party. al-jāriya here is the rider herself. sallama ʿalā, “to greet (someone)”, literally “to say salām upon”: the verb takes ʿalā.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَهَا عَلِيُّ ابْنُ بَكَّارٍ سَلَبَتْ عَقْلَهُ وَأَرَادَ الْقِيَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā ʿaliyyu ibnu bakkārin salabat ʿaqlahu wa-arāda al-qiyāma
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī son of Bakkār saw-her, she-robbed his-mind, and he-wanted the rising.
sentences.i: When ʿAlī ibn Bakkār saw her, she robbed him of his wits, and he made to get up and leave.
sentences.n: The print writes رأها for رآها, raʾāhā, “he saw her”, without the madda. Here ibn keeps its alif (علي ابن بكار), unlike two sentences above.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ اجْلِسْ مَكَانَكَ نَحْنُ جِئْنَا صَدَّكَ وَأَنْتَ تَرُوحُ هَذَا مَاهُوَ إِنْصَافٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu ijlis makānaka naḥnu jiʾnā ṣaddaka wa-anta tarūḥu hādhā mā huwa inṣāfun
sentences.l: And she-said to-him: Sit (in) your-place! We, we-came [towards-you], and you go-off? This not-is fairness.
sentences.i: She said to him, “Stay where you are. We came here for you, and you go off? That is hardly fair.”
sentences.n: The print's صدك is doubtful. It is pointed here as ṣaddaka, an adverb “facing you, in your direction” (ṣadd, like ṣadad, “the side that faces”); it may instead be a slip for قصدك, qaṣdaka, “seeking you, on your account”. The sense is much the same either way. rāḥa, “to go off”, is a colloquial verb. mā huwa inṣāf, “this is not fair”: negation by mā plus a pronoun, a Middle Arabic pattern (spoken mā-hū); the print runs ماهو together.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَاللَّهِ يَاسِتِّي إِنِّي هَارِبٌ مِمَّا رَأَيْتُ وَلِسَانُ الْحَالِ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-allāhi yā sittī innī hāribun mimmā raʾaytu wa-lisānu al-ḥāli yaqūlu
sentences.l: And he-said: By God, O my-lady, I (am) fleeing from what I-saw! And the tongue of the state (was) saying:
sentences.i: He said, “By God, my lady, I am running away from what I have seen!” And his plight spoke for him:
sentences.n: sittī, “my lady”, the colloquial form of sayyidatī; the print runs the vocative yā onto it (ياستي). lisān al-ḥāl, “the tongue of the state”, what a person's condition says without words: the verses that follow are what his look declared. The damma of رأيتُ is the print's own.

sentences.t:
هِيَ الشَّمْسُ مَسْكَنُهَا فِي السَّمَاءِ * فَعَزِّا لْفُوَادَ عَزَاءًا جَمِيْلًا
فَلَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ اِلَيْهَا الصُّعُوْ * دَوَلَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ اِلَيْكَ النُّزُوْلَا
sentences.tr:
hiya al-shamsu maskanuhā fī al-samāʾi * fa-ʿazzi al-fuwāda ʿazāʾan jamīlā
fa-lan tastaṭīʿa ilayhā al-ṣuʿū * da wa-lan tastaṭīʿa ilayka al-nuzūlā
sentences.l:
She (is) the sun, her-dwelling (is) in the sky, * so console the heart a consolation beautiful;
for you-will-not be-able to-her the ascen- * -t, and she-will-not be-able to-you the descending.
sentences.i:
She is the sun, whose dwelling is in the sky: so comfort your heart with a seemly patience,
for you can never climb up to her, and she can never come down to you.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed. The print sets the space of فعزّ الفؤاد after the alif (فَعَزِّا لْفُوَادَ) and writes al-fuʾād, “the heart”, without its hamza; عَزَاءًا writes the alif of the tanwīn after the hamza. al-ṣuʿūd, “the ascent”, is split by the caesura, its last letter opening the second hemistich (الصُّعُوْ * دَ), a licence the metre allows. tastaṭīʿa is “you can” in the first hemistich and “she can” in the second: the same form serves both persons.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ ذَلِكَ تَبَسَّمَتْ وَقَالَتْ لِأَبِي الْحَسَنِ مَا اسْمُ هَذَا الشَّابِّ وَمِنْ أَيْنَ هُوَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat dhālika tabassamat wa-qālat li-abī al-ḥasani mā ismu hādhā al-shābbi wa-min ayna huwa
sentences.l: And when she-heard that, she-smiled and said to Abū al-Ḥasan: What (is) the name of this youth, and from where (is) he?
sentences.i: When she heard this she smiled, and said to Abū al-Ḥasan, “What is this young man's name, and where is he from?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا هَذَا غَرِيبٌ فَقَالَتْ مِنْ أَيِّ الْبِلَادِ فَقَالَ إِنَّهُ ابْنُ مَلِكِ الْعَجَمِ وَاسْمُهُ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَالْغَرِيبُ يَجِبُ إِكْرَامُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā hādhā gharībun fa-qālat min ayyi al-bilādi fa-qāla innahu ibnu maliki al-ʿajami wa-ismuhu ʿaliyyu ibnu bakkārin wa-al-gharību yajibu ikrāmuhu
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: This (is) a stranger. And she-said: From which of the lands? And he-said: He (is) the son of the king of the Persians, and his-name (is) ʿAlī son of Bakkār; and the stranger, there-is-due his-honouring.
sentences.i: He told her, “He is a stranger here.” “From what country?” she asked. He said, “He is the son of the king of Persia, and his name is ʿAlī ibn Bakkār; and a stranger must be shown honour.”
sentences.n: al-gharību yajibu ikrāmuhu, “the stranger, his honouring is due”: the topic is put first and taken up again by the pronoun of ikrāmuhu. The shadda of ايّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِذَا جَاءَتْكَ جَارِيَتِي تَأْتِي بِهِ عِنْدِي فَقَالَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ عَلَى الرَّأْسِ وَالْعَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu idhā jāʾatka jāriyatī taʾtī bihi ʿindī fa-qāla abū al-ḥasani ʿalā al-raʾsi wa-al-ʿayni
sentences.l: And she-said to-him: When there-comes-to-you my-slave-girl, you-bring him to-me. And Abū al-Ḥasan said: On the head and the eye!
sentences.i: She said to him, “When my maid comes to you, bring him to me.” Abū al-Ḥasan said, “Gladly; on my head and my eyes be it.”
sentences.n: The print has تأني, a misprint for تأتي, corrected here. atā bi-, “to come with”, is “to bring”: the verb takes bi- for what is brought. taʾtī bihi, “you bring him”, is an indicative used as a request, as in speech; ʿindī, “to where I am”. ʿalā al-raʾs wa-al-ʿayn, “on the head and the eye”, is a formula of willing obedience.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتْ وَتَوَجَّهَتْ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat wa-tawajjahat ilā ḥāli sabīlihā
sentences.l: Then she-rose and turned-herself to the state of her-way.
sentences.i: Then she rose and went on her way.
sentences.n: ilā ḥāl sabīlihā, “to the state of her way”, a set phrase for going off about one's business. The shadda of توجّهت is the print's own.

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهَا
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihā
sentences.l: This (is) what was of her-affair.
sentences.i: So much for her.
sentences.n: The storyteller's formula for leaving one thread of the story to take up another.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ عَلِيِّ ابْنِ بَكَّارٍ فَإِنَّهُ صَارَ لَايَعْرِفُ مَا يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin fa-innahu ṣāra lā yaʿrifu mā yaqūlu
sentences.l: And as-for what was of the affair of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, he became not-knowing what he-should-say.
sentences.i: As for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, he no longer knew what to say.
sentences.n: wa-ammā mā kāna min amr …, “as for what there was of the affair of …”, the storyteller's formula for turning to another character; ammā is answered by fa- (fa-innahu). The print writes ibn with its alif here, although it stands between two names, and runs لا يعرف together as one word.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ جَاءَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ إِلَى أَبِى الْحَسَنِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّ سِتِّي تَطْلُبُكَ أَنْتَ وَرَفِيقَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda sāʿatin jāʾati al-jāriyatu ilā Abī al-Ḥasani wa-qālat lahu inna sittī taṭlubuka anta wa-rafīqaka
sentences.l: And after an hour the slave-girl came to Abū al-Ḥasan and said to him: Indeed my-lady seeks-you, you and your-companion.
sentences.i: After a while the slave-girl came to Abū al-Ḥasan and said to him, “My lady asks for you, you and your companion.”
sentences.n: sāʿa, “hour”, often just “a while”. sittī, “my lady”, the colloquial form of sayyidatī: Shams al-Nahār, whom the girl serves. anta wa-rafīqaka: the free pronoun anta picks up the object -ka so that “your companion” can be added to it.

sentences.t: فَنَهَضَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ وَأَخَذَ مَعَهُ عَلِيًّا بْنَ بَكَّارٍ وَسَارَا إِلَى دَارِ هَارُونَ الرَّشِيدِ
sentences.tr: fa-nahaḍa Abū al-Ḥasani wa-akhadha maʿahu ʿAliyyan bna Bakkārin wa-sārā ilā dāri Hārūna al-Rashīdi
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan rose and took with-him ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and the-two went to the house of Hārūn al-Rashīd.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan rose and took ʿAlī ibn Bakkār with him, and the two of them went to the palace of Hārūn al-Rashīd.
sentences.n: The print runs Abū al-Ḥasan together as one word (ابوالحسن). sārā, “the two went”, is dual. dār, “house”, here the Caliph's residence.

sentences.t: فَأَدْخَلَتْهُمَا فِي مَقْصُورَةٍ وَأَجْلَسَتْهُمَا فَتَحَدَّثَا سَاعَةً وَإِذَا بِالْمَوَائِدِ وُضِعَتْ قُدَّامَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-adkhalathumā fī maqṣūratin wa-ajlasathumā fa-taḥaddathā sāʿatan wa-idhā bi-al-mawāʾidi wuḍiʿat quddāmahumā
sentences.l: And she-made-the-two-enter into a chamber and seated-the-two, and the-two talked an hour; and behold, the tables were-set before-the-two.
sentences.i: She brought them into a private chamber and seated them, and they talked for a while; and then tables were set before them.
sentences.n: The subject of adkhalathumā, “she brought the two in”, is the slave-girl. maqṣūra, a closed-off room, a private apartment. wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks what appears, here the tables (mawāʾid, plural of māʾida, a table or tray spread with food). The shaddas in فتحدّثا and قدّامهما are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَكَلَا وَغَسَلَا أَيْدِيَهُمَا ثُمَّ أَحْضَرَتْ لَهُمَا الشَّرَابَ فَسَكِرَا
sentences.tr: fa-akalā wa-ghasalā aydiyahumā thumma aḥḍarat lahumā al-sharāba fa-sakirā
sentences.l: And the-two ate and washed their-hands; then she-brought for-the-two the drink, and the-two became-drunk.
sentences.i: They ate and washed their hands; then she brought them wine, and they grew drunk.
sentences.n: sharāb, “drink”, in the Nights usually wine, as fa-sakirā, “and they became drunk”, shows.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَتْهُمَا بِالْقِيَامِ فَقَامَا مَعَهَا فَأَدْخَلَتْهُمَا مَقْصُورَةً أُخْرَى مُرَكَّبَةً عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَعْمِدَةٍ وَهِيَ مَفْرُوشَةٌ بِأَنْوَاعِ الْفُرُشِ مُزَيَّنَةٌ بِأَنْوَاعِ الزِّينَةِ كَأَنَّهَا مِنْ مَقَاصِيرِ الْجِنَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma amarathumā bi-al-qiyāmi fa-qāmā maʿahā fa-adkhalathumā maqṣūratan ukhrā murakkabatan ʿalā arbaʿati aʿmidatin wa-hiya mafrūshatun bi-anwāʿi al-furushi muzayyanatun bi-anwāʿi al-zīnati ka-annahā min maqāṣīri al-jināni
sentences.l: Then she-ordered-the-two to rising, and the-two rose with-her, and she-made-the-two-enter another chamber, built on four pillars; and it (was) spread with kinds of the furnishings, adorned with kinds of the adornment, as-if it (were) of the chambers of the Gardens.
sentences.i: Then she bade them rise, and they went with her, and she brought them into another chamber raised on four pillars, spread with every kind of carpet and decked with every kind of ornament, as though it were one of the pavilions of Paradise.
sentences.n: amara bi-, “order (something)”: the verb takes the thing ordered with bi-. mafrūsha bi-anwāʿ al-furush, muzayyana bi-anwāʿ al-zīna: a rhymed pair. al-jinān, “the Gardens”, plural of janna, Paradise.

sentences.t: فَانْدَهَشَا مِمَّا عَايَنَا مِنَ التُّحَفِ
sentences.tr: fa-indahashā mimmā ʿāyanā mina al-tuḥafi
sentences.l: And the-two were-amazed at-what the-two beheld of the rarities.
sentences.i: They were dazzled by the rare and precious things they saw.
sentences.n: indahasha, “be astonished”, a colloquial seventh form beside Classical dahisha. tuḥaf, plural of tuḥfa, “a rare, precious object”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُمَا يَتَفَرَّجَانِ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْغَرَائِبِ وَإِذَا بِعَشْرِ جَوَارٍ أَقْبَلْنَ كَأَنَّهُنَّ الْأَقْمَارُ يَتَمَايَلْنَ عُجْبًا يُدْهِشْنَ الْأَبْصَارَ وَيُحَيِّرْنَ الْأَفْكَارَ وَاصْطَفَفْنَ كَأَنَّهُنَّ مِنْ حُورِ الْجِنَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā yatafarrajāni ʿalā hādhihi al-gharāʾibi wa-idhā bi-ʿashri jawārin aqbalna ka-annahunna al-aqmāru yatamāyalna ʿujban yudhishna al-abṣāra wa-yuḥayyirna al-afkāra wa-iṣṭafafna ka-annahunna min ḥūri al-jināni
sentences.l: And while the-two were-gazing at these wonders, behold, ten slave-girls came-forward, as-if they (were) the moons, swaying in-pride; they-dazzle the eyes and bewilder the thoughts; and they-ranged-themselves-in-a-row as-if they (were) of the houris of the Gardens.
sentences.i: While they were gazing at these marvels, ten slave-girls came in, like so many moons, swaying proudly, dazzling the eye and bewildering the mind; and they ranged themselves in a row, as though they were houris of Paradise.
sentences.n: The print has الاتمار, a misprint for الاقمار, corrected here. tafarraja ʿalā, “look on at, enjoy the sight of”, a colloquial verb. wa-idhā bi-ʿashr jawārin, “and behold, ten girls”: after idhā of surprise the bi- only marks what appears. jawārin, plural of jāriya, “slave-girl”. yudhishna al-abṣār wa-yuḥayyirna al-afkār is a rhymed pair; the shadda in يحيّرن is the print's own. ḥūr, the dark-eyed maidens of Paradise.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ بُرْهَةٍ وَإِذَا بِعَشْرِ جَوَارٍ أُخْرَى أَقْبَلْنَ فَسَلَّمْنَ عَلَيْهِمَا وَبِأَيْدِيهِنَّ الْعِيدَانُ وَآلَاتُ اللَّهْوِ وَالطَّرَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda burhatin wa-idhā bi-ʿashri jawārin ukhrā aqbalna fa-sallamna ʿalayhimā wa-bi-aydīhinna al-ʿīdānu wa-ālātu al-lahwi wa-al-ṭarabi
sentences.l: And after a while, behold, ten other slave-girls came-forward and gave-greeting upon-the-two, and in their-hands the lutes and the instruments of the diversion and the delight.
sentences.i: After a little while ten more slave-girls came in and greeted them, carrying lutes and instruments of pleasure and music.
sentences.n: sallama ʿalā, “greet”: the greeting is wished “upon” the one greeted. ʿīdān, plural of ʿūd, “lute”. ṭarab, the rapture music stirs, and so music itself.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسْنَ كُلُّهُنَّ وَأَصْلَحْنَ الْأَوْتَارَ وَقُمْنَ بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمَا يَضْرِبْنَ بِالْعِيدَانِ وَيُغَنِّينَ وَيُنْشِدْنَ الْأَشْعَارَ وَكُلُّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِنْهُنَّ فِتْنَةٌ لِلْعِبَادِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasna kulluhunna wa-aṣlaḥna al-awtāra wa-qumna bayna aydīhimā yaḍribna bi-al-ʿīdāni wa-yughannīna wa-yunshidna al-ashʿāra wa-kullu wāḥidatin minhunna fitnatun li-al-ʿibādi
sentences.l: And they-sat, all-of-them, and set-right the strings, and stood between the-hands-of-the-two, striking on the lutes and singing and reciting the verses; and every one of-them (was) a temptation to the servants (of God).
sentences.i: They all sat down and tuned the strings; then they stood before the two men, playing on the lutes, singing and reciting verses, and every one of them was a temptation to the servants of God.
sentences.n: aṣlaḥa, “put right”, of strings “tune”. qāma bayna yaday, “stand between the hands of”, means to stand in attendance before someone. ḍaraba bi-, “strike on”, is how one plays a lute: the bi- takes the instrument. fitna, “trial, temptation”; al-ʿibād, “the servants (of God)”, mankind. The shadda in يغنّين is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَاهُمَا كَذَلِكَ وَإِذَا بِعَشْرِ جَوَارٍ مِثْلِهِنَّ كَوَاعِبَ أَتْرَابٍ سُودِ الْعُيُونِ مُوَرَّدَاتِ الْخُدُودِ مَقْرُونَاتِ الْحَوَاجِبِ نَاعِسَاتِ الْأَطْرَافِ فِتْنَةٍ لِلْعَابِدِينَ وَنُزْهَةٍ لِلنَّاظِرِينَ وَعَلَيْهِنَّ مِنْ أَنْوَاعِ الْحَرِيرِ الْمُلَوَّنِ وَالْحُلَلِ مَا يُدْهِشُ الْعَقْلَ وَيُحَيِّرُةُ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-ʿashri jawārin mithlihinna kawāʿiba atrābin sūdi al-ʿuyūni muwarradāti al-khudūdi maqrūnāti al-ḥawājibi nāʿisāti al-aṭrāfi fitnatin li-al-ʿābidīna wa-nuzhatin li-al-nāẓirīna wa-ʿalayhinna min anwāʿi al-ḥarīri al-mulawwani wa-al-ḥulali mā yudhishu al-ʿaqla wa-yuḥayyiruhu
sentences.l: And while the-two (were) thus, behold, ten slave-girls like-them, full-breasted, of-an-age, black of the eyes, rosy of the cheeks, joined of the eyebrows, drowsy of the glances, a temptation to the worshippers and a delight to the beholders; and upon-them, of kinds of the coloured silk and the robes, what amazes the mind and bewilders-it.
sentences.i: While they were so, ten more slave-girls came in like them, high-breasted maidens all of an age, black-eyed and rosy-cheeked, their eyebrows meeting, their glances languid, a temptation to the devout and a delight to all who looked on; and they wore coloured silks and robes of every kind, enough to dazzle and bewilder the mind.
sentences.n: The print runs بينما هما together. kawāʿib atrāb, “full-breasted, of like age”, is the Qurʾān's description of the maidens of Paradise (78:33). Eyebrows that meet were a mark of beauty; aṭrāf, plural of ṭarf, “glance”. The run of rhymes ends al-ʿābidīn / al-nāẓirīn. The print writes the pronoun of yuḥayyiruhu, “bewilders it”, with a tāʾ marbūṭa (يحيرة for يحيّره), a habit of this edition. The shaddas in مورّدات and الملوّن are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَوَقَفْنَ بِالْبَابِ وَجَاءَ مِنْ بَعْدِهِنَّ عَشْرُ جَوَارٍ أُخْرَى أَحْسَنَ مِنْهُنَّ وَعَلَيْهِنَّ مِنَ الْمَلَابِسِ الْفَاخِرَةِ مَا لَا يَدْخُلُ تَحْتَ وَصْفٍ فَوَقَفْنَ أَيْضًا بِالْبَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-waqafna bi-al-bābi wa-jāʾa min baʿdihinna ʿashru jawārin ukhrā aḥsana minhunna wa-ʿalayhinna mina al-malābisi al-fākhirati mā lā yadkhulu taḥta waṣfin fa-waqafna ayḍan bi-al-bābi
sentences.l: And they-stood at the door; and there-came after-them ten other slave-girls, more-beautiful than-them, and upon-them of the splendid garments what does-not enter under description; and they-stood also at the door.
sentences.i: They stood at the door; and after them came ten more slave-girls, lovelier still, in splendid garments past all describing, and they too stood at the door.
sentences.n: bi-al-bāb, “at the door”: bi- of place. jāʾa is masculine before a feminine plural subject: a verb that comes first need not agree. mā lā yadkhulu taḥta waṣf, “what does not come under description”, that is, beyond describing.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَ مِنَ الْبَابِ عِشْرُونَ جَارِيَةً وَبَيْنَهُنَّ جَارِيَةٌ اسْمُهَا شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ كَأَنَّهَا الْقَمَرُ بَيْنَ النُّجُومِ وَهِيَ تَتَمَايَلُ عُجْبًا وَدَلَالًا وَهِيَ مُتَوَشِّحَةٌ بِفَاضِلِ شَعْرِهَا وَعَلَيْهَا ثَوْبٌ أَزْرَقُ وَإِزَارٌ مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ بِطِرَازَاتٍ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَالْجَوْهَرِ وَفِي وَسَطِهَا حِيَاصَةٌ مُرَصَّعَةٌ بِأَنْوَاعِ الْجَوَاهِرِ
sentences.tr: thumma kharaja mina al-bābi ʿishrūna jāriyatan wa-baynahunna jāriyatun ismuhā Shamsu al-Nahāri ka-annahā al-qamaru bayna al-nujūmi wa-hiya tatamāyalu ʿujban wa-dalālan wa-hiya mutawashshiḥatun bi-fāḍili shaʿrihā wa-ʿalayhā thawbun azraqu wa-izārun mina al-ḥarīri bi-ṭirāzātin mina al-dhahabi wa-al-jawhari wa-fī wasaṭihā ḥiyāṣatun muraṣṣaʿatun bi-anwāʿi al-jawāhiri
sentences.l: Then there-came-out from the door twenty slave-girls, and among-them a slave-girl, her-name Shams al-Nahār, as-if she (were) the moon among the stars; and she swaying in-pride and coquetry, and she wrapped with the overflow of her-hair; and upon-her a blue gown and a wrap of the silk with bands of the gold and the jewels, and at her-middle a girdle studded with kinds of the gems.
sentences.i: Then twenty slave-girls came out through the door, and among them was a girl named Shams al-Nahār, like the moon among the stars, swaying with pride and coquetry, mantled in the long fall of her hair. She wore a blue gown and a silk wrap with borders worked in gold and jewels, and about her waist a girdle set with every kind of gem.
sentences.n: Shams al-Nahār, “Sun of the Day”. mutawashshiḥa bi-, “wearing (something) as a sash”: her hair is long enough to wrap her, fāḍil being “what is left over, the excess”. ṭirāz, an embroidered band on a garment. ḥiyāṣa, a girdle or belt.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تَتَبَخْتَرُ وَتَتَمَايَلُ حَتَّى جَلَسَتْ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal tatabakhtaru wa-tatamāyalu ḥattā jalasat ʿalā al-sarīri
sentences.l: And she-did-not cease strutting and swaying until she-sat on the couch.
sentences.i: She came on, strutting and swaying, until she sat down upon the couch.
sentences.n: lam tazal with an imperfect, “she did not cease …”, that is, “she kept on …”. sarīr, a raised couch or throne.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأٰهَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ أَنْشَدَ هَذِهِ الْأَشْعَارَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā ʿAliyyu bnu Bakkārin anshada hādhihi al-ashʿāra
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī ibn Bakkār saw her, he recited these verses:
sentences.n: The print spells raʾāhā, “he saw her”, as رأها, without the long ā that the Classical spelling رآها writes; the dagger alif supplies it.

sentences.t:
اِنَّ هٰذِيْ هِيَ اِبْتِدَاءُ سَقَامِيْ * وَتَمَادِيْ وَجْدِيْ وَطُوْلُ غَرَامِيْ
عِنْدَهَا قَدْ رَأَيْتُ نَفْسِيَ ذَابَتْ * مِنْ وُلُوْعِيْ بِهَا وَبَرَى عِظَامِيْ
sentences.tr:
inna hādhī hiya ibtidāʾu saqāmī * wa-tamādī wajdī wa-ṭūlu gharāmī
ʿindahā qad raʾaytu nafsiya dhābat * min wulūʿī bihā wa-barā ʿiẓāmī
sentences.l:
Indeed this-one, she (is) the beginning of my-sickness * and the drawing-out of my-passion and the length of my-love-torment;
beside-her I have seen my-soul melted * from my-ardour for-her, and (it) has-pared-thin my-bones.
sentences.i:
She, she is the beginning of my sickness, * the long drawing-out of my passion, my lasting love-pain;
before her I have seen my soul melt away * with longing for her, and my bones are worn thin.
sentences.n: hādhī is a by-form of the feminine demonstrative hādhihi. tamādī, “going on, being drawn out”. barā, “pare, whittle”, as one pares a reed pen; the subject is left unstated, the passion or the woman herself. The print writes the first word with a kasra under a bare alif (اِنَّ), as it does اِبْتِدَاءُ.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ لِأَبِي الْحَسَنِ لَوْ عَمِلْتَ مَعِي خَيْرًا كُنْتَ أَخْبَرْتَنِي بِهَذِهِ الْأُمُورِ قَبْلَ الدُّخُولِ هُنَا لِأَجْلِ أَنْ أُوَطِّنَ نَفْسِي وَأُصَبِّرَهَا عَلَى مَا أَصَابَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi qāla li-Abī al-Ḥasani law ʿamilta maʿī khayran kunta akhbartanī bi-hādhihi al-umūri qabla al-dukhūli hunā li-ajli an uwaṭṭina nafsī wa-uṣabbirahā ʿalā mā aṣābahā
sentences.l: And when he-finished from his-poetry, he-said to Abū al-Ḥasan: If you-had-done with-me a kindness, you-would-have told-me of these matters before the entering here, for-the-sake that I-might-settle my-soul and make-it-patient over what befell-it.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses he said to Abū al-Ḥasan, “If you had wished me well, you would have told me of all this before we came in here, so that I could have steeled myself and taught my heart to bear what has befallen it.”
sentences.n: law … kunta akhbartanī: the answer to law comes without the Classical la-, as often in this text. akhbara bi-, “inform of”: the verb takes its matter with bi-. al-dukhūl hunā, “coming in here”, where Classical would say ilā hunā: a colloquial turn. waṭṭana nafsahu ʿalā, “resign oneself to, steel oneself for”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى
sentences.tr: thumma bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā
sentences.l: Then he-wept and moaned and complained.
sentences.n: anna, “moan, groan”; the shadda in وانّ is the print's own. bakā and ishtakā rhyme.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ يَا أَخِي أَنَا مَا أَرَدْتُ لَكَ إِلَّا الْخَيْرَ وَلَكِنْ خَشِيتُ أَنْ أُعْلِمَكَ بِذَلِكَ فَيَلْحَقَكَ مِنَ الْوَجْدِ مَا يَصُدُّكَ عَنْ لِقَائِهَا وَيَحِيلُ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani yā akhī anā mā aradtu laka illā al-khayra wa-lākin khashītu an uʿlimaka bi-dhālika fa-yalḥaqaka mina al-wajdi mā yaṣudduka ʿan liqāʾihā wa-yaḥīlu baynaka wa-baynahā
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to him: O my-brother, I, I-did-not want for-you except the good; but I-feared that I-inform-you of that, and there-overtake-you of the passion what turns-you-away from meeting-her and comes between-you and between-her.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said to him, “Brother, I wanted nothing for you but good. But I was afraid that if I told you, such passion would come over you as would keep you from meeting her and stand between you and her.
sentences.n: aʿlama bi-, “inform of”: the verb takes its matter with bi-. yaḥīlu bayna, “come between”, stands where Classical has yaḥūlu (from ḥāla, yaḥūlu): the print has a yāʾ for the wāw, either a by-form of the spoken language or a slip; it is kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَطِبْ نَفْسًا وَقَرَّ عَيْنًا فَهِيَ نَحْوَكَ مُقْبِلَةٌ وَلِلِقَائِكَ مُتَوَصِّلَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭib nafsan wa-qarra ʿaynan fa-hiya naḥwaka muqbilatun wa-li-liqāʾika mutawaṣṣilatun
sentences.l: So be-good of soul and be-cool of eye, for she (is) toward-you turning, and to your-meeting seeking-the-way.
sentences.i: So take heart and be glad, for she is turning toward you and seeking the way to meet you.”
sentences.n: ṭib nafsan, “be good of soul”, and qarra ʿaynan, “be cool of eye”: two set phrases for “be glad”, the noun after each imperative saying in what respect. muqbila and mutawaṣṣila rhyme. The shadda in وقرّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ مَا اسْمُ هَذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyu bnu Bakkārin mā ismu hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati
sentences.l: And ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said: What (is) the name of this young-girl?
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār asked, “What is this girl's name?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ تُسَمَّى شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ وَهِيَ مِنْ مَحَاظِي أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ هَارُونَ الرَّشِيدِ وَهَذَا الْمَكَانُ قَصْرُ الْخِلَافَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani tusammā Shamsa al-Nahāri wa-hiya min maḥāẓī amīri al-muʾminīna Hārūna al-Rashīdi wa-hādhā al-makānu qaṣru al-khilāfati
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to him: She-is-named Shams al-Nahār, and she (is) of the favourites of the Commander of the Faithful, Hārūn al-Rashīd, and this place (is) the palace of the Caliphate.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan told him, “She is called Shams al-Nahār. She is one of the favourites of the Commander of the Faithful, Hārūn al-Rashīd, and this place is the palace of the Caliphate.”
sentences.n: tusammā, “she is named”, takes the name as its object (Shamsa). maḥāẓī, plural of maḥẓiyya, a concubine in favour with her master.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ جَلَسَتْ وَتَأَمَّلَتْ مَحَاسِنَ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَتَأَمَّلَ هُوَ أَيْضًا حُسْنَهَا فَاشْتَغَلَا بِحُبِّ بَعْضِهِمَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna Shamsa al-Nahāri jalasat wa-taʾammalat maḥāsina ʿAliyyi bni Bakkārin wa-taʾammala huwa ayḍan ḥusnahā fa-ishtaghalā bi-ḥubbi baʿḍihimā
sentences.l: Then Shams al-Nahār sat and contemplated the beauties of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and he also contemplated her-beauty, and the-two became-occupied with love of each-other.
sentences.i: Then Shams al-Nahār sat and gazed upon ʿAlī ibn Bakkār's beauty, and he upon hers, and they were wholly taken up with love of one another.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it was that)”, a narrative restart. ishtaghala bi-, “be busy with, be absorbed in”. bi-ḥubbi baʿḍihimā, “with love of one another”, is a loose colloquial reciprocal. The print writes taʾammalat with its hamza and taʾammala without.

sentences.t: فَأَمَرَتِ الْجَوَارِيَ أَنْ تَجْلِسَ كُلُّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِنْهُنَّ فِي مَكَانِهَا عَلَى سَرِيرٍ فَجَلَسَتْ كُلُّ وَاحِدَةٍ قُبَالَ طَاقَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-amarati al-jawāriya an tajlisa kullu wāḥidatin minhunna fī makānihā ʿalā sarīrin fa-jalasat kullu wāḥidatin qubāla ṭāqatin
sentences.l: And she-ordered the slave-girls that every one of-them sit in her-place on a couch; and every one sat facing a window.
sentences.i: She ordered the girls each to take her seat on a couch in her own place, and each sat facing a window.
sentences.n: qubāla, “facing, opposite”. ṭāqa, a window or arched niche in a wall.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَتْهُنَّ بِالْغِنَاءِ فَأَخَذَتْ وَاحِدَةٌ مِنْهُنَّ الْعُودَ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-amarathunna bi-al-ghināʾi fa-akhadhat wāḥidatun minhunna al-ʿūda wa-anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: And she-ordered-them to the singing, and one of-them took the lute and recited, saying:
sentences.i: Then she bade them sing, and one of them took up the lute and sang these words:
sentences.n: amara bi-, “order (something)”: the bi- takes the thing ordered. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”, introduces verse; the song follows.

sentences.t:
اَعِدِ الرِّسَالَةً ثَانِيَهْ * وَخُذِ الْجَوَابَ عَلَانِيَهْ
وَاِلَيْكَ يَا مَلِكُ الْمِلَا * حِ وَقَفْتُ اَشْكُوْحَا لِيَهْ
مَوْلَايَ يَاقَلْبِي الْعَزِيزُ * وَيَا حَيَاتِي الْغَالِيَهْ
اِنْعَمْ عَلَيَّ بِقُبْلَةٍ * هِبَةً وَاِلَّا عَارِبَهْ
وَاَرُدُّهَا لَكَ لَاعَدِمْتَ * بِعَيْنِهَا وَكَمَا هِيَهْ
وَاِذَا اَرَدَّتَّ زِيَادَةً * خُذْهَا وَنَفْسُكَ رَاضِيَهْ
يَامُلْبِسِي ثَوْبَ الضَّنَى * يُهْنِيْكَ ثَوْبُ الْعَافِيَهْ
sentences.tr:
aʿidi al-risālata thāniyah * wa-khudhi al-jawāba ʿalāniyah
wa-ilayka yā maliku al-milā * ḥi waqaftu ashkū ḥāliyah
mawlāya yā qalbī al-ʿazīzu * wa-yā ḥayātī al-ghāliyah
anʿim ʿalayya bi-qublatin * hibatan wa-illā ʿāribah
wa-aruddu-hā laka lā ʿadimta * bi-ʿaynihā wa-ka-mā hiyah
wa-idhā aradtta ziyādatan * khudhhā wa-nafsuka rāḍiyah
yā mulbisī thawba al-ḍanā * yuhnīka thawbu al-ʿāfiyah
sentences.l:
Repeat the message a-second-time * and take the answer openly!
And to-you, O king of the fair-ones, * I-have-stood complaining-of my-state.
My-master, O my-heart, the dear-one, * and O my-life, the precious-one,
Bestow upon-me a kiss * as-a-gift, or-else (as) a-loan,
And I-will-return-it to-you — may-you-not-be-bereft! — * its-very-self and as it is;
And if you-want an-increase, * take-it, and your-soul content.
O clother-of-me (in) the garment of the wasting, * may-it-be-wholesome-to-you, the garment of the well-being!
sentences.i:
Send the message once again, and take your answer openly.
To you, O king of all the fair, I come to make my plaint.
My lord, O my dear heart, O my precious life,
grant me a kiss, as a gift, or else on loan,
and I will give it back to you (may you never lack!) the very same, just as it was;
and if you want more, take it, with a willing heart.
You who have clothed me in the robe of wasting sickness, may the robe of health be yours to enjoy!
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own and is kept as printed. The metre is the shortened kāmil, every line rhyming on -iyah with the pausal h, so that ʿalāniya, ḥāliya, ghāliya are read ʿalāniyah, ḥāliyah, ghāliyah. Several things in the print are odd. الرِّسَالَةً carries the tanwīn of an indefinite noun on a word with the article; it surely stands for al-risālata. اَشْكُوْحَا لِيَهْ is set with the word break in the wrong place: it stands for ashkū ḥāliyah, “I complain of my state”, ḥālī with the extra pausal -yah of the rhyme. يَا مَلِكُ has a ḍamma where the vocative of a construct phrase takes the accusative, malika; the word al-milāḥ, “the fair ones”, is broken across the two hemistichs (الْمِلَا * حِ). عَارِبَهْ makes no sense here and almost certainly stands for ʿāriyah, “a loan”, the dot of yāʾ printed as that of bāʾ: “as a gift or else on loan” is the sense the next line confirms. lā ʿadimta, “may you not be bereft”, is a stock blessing dropped into the sentence. اَرَدَّتَّ is pointed with two shaddas, apparently to show the d of arad- assimilated to the t of the ending, i.e. aradta pronounced arattā; the sense is simply “you want”. يُهْنِيْكَ stands for the wish yahnīka or yuhanniʾka, “may it do you good”, written with no hamza. The speaker is the singing girl addressing ʿAlī ibn Bakkār on behalf of her mistress.

sentences.t: فَطَرِبَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَقَالَ لَهَا زِيدِينِي مِنْ مِثْلِ هَذَا الشِّعْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭariba ʿAliyyu bnu Bakkārin wa-qāla lahā zīdīnī min mithli hādhā al-shiʿri
sentences.l: And ʿAlī ibn Bakkār was-moved-with-delight, and he-said to-her: Add-for-me of the-like of this poetry!
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār was carried away with delight and said to her, “Give me more poetry like this.”
sentences.n: The print has زبديني, a misprint for زيديني, corrected here. zīdīnī, “give me more”, the feminine imperative of zāda with the object suffix -nī. ṭariba is to be stirred by ṭarab, the rapture that music and poetry bring on.

sentences.t: فَحَرَّكَتِ الْأَوْتَارَ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَشْعَارَ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥarrakati al-awtāra wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-ashʿāra
sentences.l: So she-moved the strings and she-recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: So she set the strings astir and sang these verses:
sentences.n: al-awtār, “the strings”, and al-ashʿār, “the verses”, rhyme: a small piece of sajʿ to lead into the song. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”, is the stock formula that introduces every poem in the Nights.

sentences.t:
مِنْ كَثْرَةِ الْبُعْدِ يَاحَبِيبِي * عَلَّمْتَ طُولَ الْبُكَا عُيُونِي
يَاحَظَّ عَيْنِي وَيَامُنَاهَا * وَمُنْتَهَى غَايَتِي وَدِينِي
اِرْثِ لِمَنْ طَرْفُهُ غَرِيقٌ * فِي عَبْرَةِ الْوَالِهِ الْحَزِينِ
sentences.tr:
min kathrati al-buʿdi yā ḥabībī * ʿallamta ṭūla al-bukā ʿuyūnī
yā ḥaẓẓa ʿaynī wa-yā munāhā * wa-muntahā ghāyatī wa-dīnī
irthi li-man ṭarfuhu gharīqun * fī ʿabrati al-wālihi al-ḥazīni
sentences.l:
From the abundance of the distance, O my-beloved, * you-have-taught the length of the weeping (to) my-eyes.
O portion of my-eye and O its-wish, * and the utmost of my-aim and my-faith,
Have-pity on-him whose glance (is) drowned * in the tear of the distraught, the grieving-one!
sentences.i:
So long have you been far away, my love, that you have taught my eyes to weep without end.
O joy of my eye and all its longing, the furthest reach of my desire, my very faith,
pity one whose eye is drowning in the tears of a man distraught with grief.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. The metre is mukhallaʿ al-basīṭ, rhyming on -īnī/-īni. al-bukā is the shortened form of al-bukāʾ, “weeping”, as poets allow themselves. ḥaẓẓ ʿaynī, “the portion of my eye”, is what my eye most delights in. irthi, “have pity”, the imperative of rathā, “to mourn, to pity”, followed by li-. The print runs yā together with the next word in ياحبيبي and يامناها and ياحظ.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا قَالَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ لِجَارِيَةٍ غَيْرِهَا أَسْمِعِينَا شَيْأً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min shiʿrihā qālat Shamsu al-Nahāri li-jāriyatin ghayrihā asmiʿīnā shayʾan
sentences.l: And when she-finished from her-poetry, Shams al-Nahār said to a slave-girl other-than-her: Make-us-hear something!
sentences.i: When she had finished her poem, Shams al-Nahār said to another of the slave-girls, “Let us hear something from you.”
sentences.n: asmiʿīnā, “make us hear”, the feminine imperative of the fourth form asmaʿa with the suffix -nā. The print spells shayʾan as شيأ, with the hamza on an alif, a common spelling in this edition. ghayrihā, “other than her”, agrees with jāriya as an adjective would.

sentences.t: فَأَطْرَبَتْ بِالنَّغَمَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-aṭrabat bi-al-naghamāti wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And she-moved-(them)-to-delight with the melodies, and she-recited, saying these lines:
sentences.i: She moved them to rapture with her melodies, and sang these lines:
sentences.n: aṭrabat, “she filled (them) with ṭarab”, the fourth form of ṭariba, with no object expressed: the delight is the listeners'.

sentences.t:
سَكِرْتُ مِنْ لَحْظِهِ لَامِنْ مُدَامَتِهِ * وَمَالَ بِالنَّوْمِ عَنْ عَيْنِي تَمَايُلُهُ
فَمَا السُّلَافُ سَلَتْنِي بَلْ سَوَالِفُهُ * وَمَا الشُّمُولُ شَلَتْنِي بَلْ شَمَائِلُهُ
لَوَى بِعَزْمِي اَصْدَاغٌ لَوَيْنَ لَهُ * وَغَالَ عَقْلِي بِمَا تَحْوَى غَلَائِلُهُ
sentences.tr:
sakirtu min laḥẓihi lā min mudāmatihi * wa-māla bi-al-nawmi ʿan ʿaynī tamāyuluhu
fa-mā al-sulāfu salatnī bal sawālifuhu * wa-mā al-shamūlu shalatnī bal shamāʾiluhu
lawā bi-ʿazmī aṣdāghun lawayna lahu * wa-ghāla ʿaqlī bi-mā taḥwā ghalāʾiluhu
sentences.l:
I-became-drunk from his-glance, not from his-wine, * and his-swaying turned-aside with the sleep from my-eye.
And not the choice-wine made-me-forget, but his-side-locks, * and not the cool-wine carried-me-off, but his-qualities.
Temple-curls that-curled for-him twisted-away with my-resolve, * and what his-under-shirts contain destroyed my-reason.
sentences.i:
It was his glance that made me drunk, not his wine; his swaying gait swayed sleep away from my eyes.
No vintage wine made me forget myself, only the locks along his cheeks; no cool wine carried me away, only his graces.
The curls that curved upon his temples bent my resolve, and what his thin shirts hold has stolen away my reason.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own; the metre is basīṭ. The beloved is a youth, as often in this poetry. Every line is built on sound-play: sulāf, “the first-run wine”, salatnī, “made me forget”, sawālif, “the locks that fall along the cheeks”; shamūl, “cool wine”, shalatnī, shamāʾil, “qualities, graces”; lawā, “twisted”, lawayna, “curled”; ghāla, “destroyed”, ghalāʾil, “the fine shirts worn next to the skin”. شَلَتْنِي is obscure: it is printed for the sake of the jingle with shamūl and shamāʾil, and probably means “carried me off” or “lured me away”, from shalā/ashlā, to raise up or call on; it may stand for shaghalatnī, “held me captive”, with a letter missing, but the print is kept. تَحْوَى, “contain”, is printed with fatḥa and alif maqṣūra where Classical writes taḥwī. māla bi-, “turned (something) aside”: the bi- makes the verb transitive.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ إِنْشَادَ الْجَارِيَةِ تَنَهَّدَتْ مَلِيًّا وَأَعْجَبَهَا الشِّعْرُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat Shamsu al-Nahāri inshāda al-jāriyati tanahhadat maliyyan wa-aʿjabahā al-shiʿru
sentences.l: And when Shams al-Nahār heard the recitation of the slave-girl, she-sighed a-long-while, and the poetry pleased-her.
sentences.i: When Shams al-Nahār heard the girl's song she sighed for a long while, for the poem had touched her.
sentences.n: The shaddas in تنهّدت and مليّا are the print's own. maliyyan, “for a long while”, an adverbial accusative. aʿjabahā al-shiʿr, “the poetry pleased her”: in Arabic the thing that pleases is the subject and the person pleased the object.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَتْ جَارِيَةً أُخْرَى أَنْ تُغَنِّيَ فَأَخَذَتِ الْعُودَ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma amarat jāriyatan ukhrā an tughanniya fa-akhadhati al-ʿūda wa-anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: Then she-ordered another slave-girl that she-sing; and she-took the lute and she-recited, saying:
sentences.i: Then she ordered another girl to sing, and the girl took up the lute and sang:
sentences.n: an tughanniya, “that she should sing”: the subjunctive after an. al-ʿūd, “the lute”, the short-necked, pear-bodied instrument that gave Europe its lute.

sentences.t:
وَجْهٌ لِمِصْبَاحِ السَّمَاءِ مُبَاهِ * يَبْدُو الشَّبَابُ عَلَيْهِ رَشْحَ مِيَاهِ
رَقَمَ الْعِذَارُ غُلَالَتَيْهِ بِأَحْرُفٍ * مَعْنَى الْهَوَى فِي طَيِّهَا مُتَنَاهِ
نَادَى عَلَيْهِ الْحُسْنُ حِينَ لَقِيتُهُ * هَذَا الْمُنَمْنَمُ فِي طِرَازِ اللّٰهِ
sentences.tr:
wajhun li-miṣbāḥi al-samāʾi mubāhi * yabdū al-shabābu ʿalayhi rashḥa miyāhi
raqama al-ʿidhāru ghulālatayhi bi-aḥrufin * maʿnā al-hawā fī ṭayyihā mutanāhi
nādā ʿalayhi al-ḥusnu ḥīna laqītuhu * hādhā al-munamnamu fī ṭirāzi Allāhi
sentences.l:
A face to the lamp of the sky vying-in-glory; * the youth appears upon-it (like) a sprinkling of waters.
The cheek-down has embroidered its-two-fine-tunics with letters, * the meaning of the love in their-fold (is) reaching-its-utmost.
The beauty called-out over-him when I-met-him: * This (is) the finely-wrought-one in the embroidered-border of God!
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own; the metre is kāmil, rhyming on -āhi. miṣbāḥ al-samāʾ, “the lamp of the sky”, is the sun. mubāhin, “vying in glory with”, takes its rival with li-; mutanāhin, “reaching its limit”, similarly drops its final -ī in the indefinite. al-ʿidhār is the first down on a youth's cheek, which poets read as writing; ghulālatayhi, “his two ghulālas”, the thin under-garments, here the two cheeks as the cloth the writing is worked into. nādā ʿalayhi, “cried him out”, is what the auctioneer does with goods for sale. ṭirāz is the embroidered band of inscription on a robe of state, worked in the caliph's workshops: the youth is a piece from God's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا قَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ لِجَارِيَةٍ قَرِيبَةٍ مِنْهُ أَنْشِدِى أَنْتِ أَيَّتُهَا الْجَارِيَةُ وَأَسْمِعِينَا شَيْأً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min shiʿrihā qāla ʿAliyyu bnu Bakkārin li-jāriyatin qarībatin minhu anshidī anti ayyatuhā al-jāriyatu wa-asmiʿīnā shayʾan
sentences.l: And when she-finished from her-poetry, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said to a slave-girl near to-him: Recite, you, O you the slave-girl, and make-us-hear something!
sentences.i: When she had finished her poem, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said to a girl sitting near him, “Now you, girl, sing, and let us hear something.”
sentences.n: anshidī, “recite!”, the feminine imperative, is printed انشدى with final ى for ي, the edition's habit. anti, “you”, added after the imperative, singles her out: “you now”. ayyatuhā al-jāriyatu, “O girl”, the feminine of ayyuhā, the form of address used before a noun with the article.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتِ الْعُودَ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhati al-ʿūda wa-anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: And she-took the lute and she-recited, saying:
sentences.i: She took the lute and sang:

sentences.t:
زَمَنُ الْوِصَالِ يَضِيقُ عَنْ * هَذَا التَّمَادِي وَالدَّلَالْ
كَمْ مِنْ صُدُودٍ مُتْلِفٍ * مَا هَكَذَا اَهْلُ الْجَمَالْ
فَاسْتَغْنِمُوْا وَقْتَ السُّعُوْ * دِ بِطِيبِ سَاعَاتِ الْوِصَالْ
sentences.tr:
zamanu al-wiṣāli yaḍīqu ʿan * hādhā al-tamādī wa-al-dalāl
kam min ṣudūdin mutlifin * mā hākadhā ahlu al-jamāl
fa-staghnimū waqta al-suʿū * di bi-ṭībi sāʿāti al-wiṣāl
sentences.l:
The time of the union is-too-narrow for * this persisting and the coquetry.
How-much of turning-away ruinous! * Not like-this (are) the people of the beauty.
So take-as-spoil the time of the good-for * tunes, with the sweetness of the hours of the union!
sentences.i:
The time we have for meeting is too short for all this holding back and play of coyness.
How much deadly coldness! That is not how the beautiful should be.
Seize the hour while fortune smiles, and take the sweetness of the hours of meeting.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, including the pausal sukūn on al-dalāl, al-jamāl and al-wiṣāl, which marks the rhyme. The metre is the shortened kāmil. al-tamādī, “persisting”, here in aloofness; al-dalāl, the coquetry of a beloved who plays hard to get. kam min ṣudūdin, “how much turning-away!”, exclamatory kam with min. The word al-suʿūd, “good fortunes, lucky stars”, is broken across the hemistichs (السُّعُوْ * دِ). istaghnimū, “take as spoil”, is a masculine plural imperative addressed to the company, or to the beloved in the plural of respect.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا أَتْبَعَهَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ بِدُمُوعٍ غِزَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min shiʿrihā atbaʿahā ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin bi-dumūʿin ghizārin
sentences.l: And when she-finished from her-verse, ʿAlī son of Bakkār made-it-followed by tears abundant.
sentences.i: When she had finished her verses, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār followed them with a flood of tears.
sentences.n: atbaʿa X bi-Y, “make Y follow X”: he answered her song with weeping. ghizār, plural of ghazīr, “copious, abundant”, said of rain and tears.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ قَدْ بَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى أَحْرَقَهَا الْوَجْدُ وَالْغَرَامُ وَأَتْلَفَهَا الْوَلَهُ وَالْهُيَامُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathu Shamsu al-Nahāri qad bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā aḥraqahā al-wajdu wa-al-gharāmu wa-atlafahā al-walahu wa-al-huyāmu
sentences.l: And when Shams al-Nahār saw-him (that) he had wept and moaned and complained, there-burned-her the longing and the passion, and there-undid-her the distraction and the love-madness.
sentences.i: When Shams al-Nahār saw him weeping, moaning and lamenting, longing and passion burned her, and love's distraction and frenzy wasted her.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: bakā / ishtakā, then al-gharām / al-huyām. anna, “moan, groan” (verb, from anna yaʾinnu); the shadda in وانّ is the print's own. walah is the distraction of grief or love; huyām, the raving love-madness that drives camels and lovers alike to wander.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتْ مِنْ فَوْقِ السَّرِيرِ وَجَاءَتْ إِلَى بَابِ الْقُبَّةِ فَقَامَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَتَلَقَّاهَا وَتَعَانَقَا وَوَقَعَا مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِمَا فِي بَابِ الْقُبَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat min fawqi al-sarīri wa-jāʾat ilā bābi al-qubbati fa-qāma ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin wa-talaqqāhā wa-taʿānaqā wa-waqaʿā maghshiyyan ʿalayhimā fī bābi al-qubbati
sentences.l: And she rose from upon the couch and came to the door of the dome; and ʿAlī son of Bakkār rose and met-her, and the-two embraced, and the-two fell fainted-upon in the door of the dome.
sentences.i: She rose from the couch and came to the door of the domed chamber; ʿAlī ibn Bakkār rose and met her, and they embraced and fell down fainting together in the doorway.
sentences.n: maghshiyyan ʿalayhimā, literally “covered over, upon them both”: the passive participle of ghashiya stays singular and the pronoun carries the number, the fixed phrase for falling in a swoon. qubba, a domed pavilion or chamber.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْجَوَارِى إِلَيْهِمَا وَحَمَلْنَهُمَا وَأَدْخَلْنَهُمَا بَابَ الْقُبَّةِ وَرَشَّشْنَ عَلَيْهِمَا مَاءَ الْوَرْدِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-jawārī ilayhimā wa-ḥamalnahumā wa-adkhalnahumā bāba al-qubbati wa-rashshashna ʿalayhimā māʾa al-wardi
sentences.l: And the slave-girls rose to-the-two, and they(f.)-carried-the-two and made-the-two-enter the door of the dome, and they(f.)-sprinkled upon-the-two the water of the rose.
sentences.i: The slave-girls ran to them, lifted them, carried them in through the door of the chamber, and sprinkled rose-water over them.
sentences.n: qāma, masculine singular, before the feminine plural al-jawārī: a verb that comes first may stay in this form before a broken plural; the following verbs, ḥamalna and rashshashna, take the feminine plural -na. The shadda in ورشّشن is the print's own: rashshasha, form II, “sprinkle again and again”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَا لَمْ يَجِدَا أَبَا الْحَسَنِ وَكَانَ قَدِ اخْتَفَى فِي جَانِبِ سَرِيرٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqā lam yajidā Abā al-Ḥasani wa-kāna qadi ikhtafā fī jānibi sarīrin
sentences.l: And when the-two came-to, the-two did-not find Abū al-Ḥasan; and he had hidden himself at the side of a couch.
sentences.i: When they came to themselves they did not find Abū al-Ḥasan, for he had hidden beside a couch.
sentences.n: afāqa, “recover one's senses”, the regular word for coming out of a faint. Abā is the accusative of Abū in the name, object of yajidā. The print has sarīr without the article, “a couch”, where the next sentence says al-sarīr, “the couch”; whether it is a dropped al- or simply “a couch” cannot be told, so it is kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ أَيْنَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ فَظَهَرَ لَهَا مِنْ جَانِبِ السَّرِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ṣabiyyatu ayna Abū al-Ḥasani fa-ẓahara lahā min jānibi al-sarīri
sentences.l: And the young-lady said: Where is Abū al-Ḥasan? And he appeared to-her from the side of the couch.
sentences.i: “Where is Abū al-Ḥasan?” the young lady asked, and he came out to her from beside the couch.
sentences.n: al-ṣabiyya, “the girl, the young woman”, is Shams al-Nahār.

sentences.t: فَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَتْ أَسْأَلُ اللَّهَ أَنْ يُقْدِرَنِي عَلَى مُكَافَأَتِكَ يَاصَاحِبَ الْمَعْرُوفِ
sentences.tr: fa-sallamat ʿalayhi wa-qālat asʾalu Allāha an yuqdiranī ʿalā mukāfaʾatika yā ṣāḥiba al-maʿrūfi
sentences.l: And she greeted (with peace) upon-him and said: I-ask God that He-make-me-able to the repaying-of-you, O possessor of the kindness!
sentences.i: She greeted him and said, “I pray God to grant me the means of repaying you, you who have done us such kindness.”
sentences.n: aqdara X ʿalā Y, “give X power over Y, enable X to do Y”. mukāfaʾa, “requital, recompense”, here for good done. ṣāḥib al-maʿrūf, “master of the kind deed”, the benefactor. The print runs يا صاحب together as one word.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي مَابَلَغَ بِكَ الْهَوَى إِلَى غَايَةٍ إِلَّا وَعِنْدِي ضِعْفُهَا وَلَكِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَنَا غَيْرُ الصَّبْرِ عَلَى مَا أَصَابَنَا
sentences.tr: thumma aqbalat ʿalā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-qālat lahu yā sayyidī mā balagha bika al-hawā ilā ghāyatin illā wa-ʿindī ḍiʿfuhā wa-lākin lam yakun lanā ghayru al-ṣabri ʿalā mā aṣābanā
sentences.l: Then she turned to ʿAlī son of Bakkār and said to-him: O my-lord, not has-reached with-you the passion to a limit except and with-me (is) the double-of-it; but there was not for-us other-than the patience upon what has-befallen-us.
sentences.i: Then she turned to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and said, “My lord, passion has brought you to no extreme that I do not suffer twice over; but we have nothing for it except to endure what has befallen us.”
sentences.n: balagha bi-X ilā, “bring X to” (the bi- makes the verb transitive): mā balagha bika al-hawā ilā ghāyatin illā …, “passion has not brought you to any limit but …”. ḍiʿf, “the double, twice as much”. The print runs ما بلغ together.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَاللَّهِ يَاسَيِّدَتِي لَيْسَ جَمْعُ شَمْلِي بِكِ يَطِيبُ وَلَا نَظَرِي إِلَيْكِ يُطْفِئُ مَاعِنْدِي مِنَ اللَّهِيبِ وَلَا يَذْهَبُ مَاتَمَكَّنَ مِنْ حُبِّكِ فِي قَلْبِي إِلَّا بِذَهَابِ رُوحِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin wa-Allāhi yā sayyidatī laysa jamʿu shamlī biki yaṭību wa-lā naẓarī ilayki yuṭfiʾu mā ʿindī mina al-lahībi wa-lā yadhhabu mā tamakkana min ḥubbiki fī qalbī illā bi-dhahābi rūḥī
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār said: By God, O my-lady, not is the gathering of my-scattered-state with-you sweet, nor my-looking at-you quenches what (is) with-me of the flame; and not goes-away what has-taken-firm-hold of love-of-you in my-heart except with the going-away of my-soul.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said, “By God, my lady, being united with you is no comfort, and looking at you does not quench the flame within me; the love of you that has taken hold of my heart will not leave it until my soul leaves me.”
sentences.n: jamʿ al-shaml, “the gathering of what is scattered”, the stock phrase for lovers' reunion. Rhyme: yaṭību / al-lahībi. The print runs together ياسيدتي, ما عندي and ما تمكن; يطفئ is printed with its hamza. laysa … yaṭību, laysa with a verb rather than a predicate noun, is common in this register.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى وَنَزَلَتْ دُمُوعُهُ عَلَى خَدِّهِ كَأَنَّهَا اللُّؤْلُؤُ الْمَنْثُورُ
sentences.tr: thumma bakā wa-nazalat dumūʿuhu ʿalā khaddihi kaʾannahā al-luʾluʾu al-manthūru
sentences.l: Then he wept, and his-tears came-down upon his-cheek as-if they (were) the pearl(s) scattered.
sentences.i: Then he wept, and his tears ran down his cheek like scattered pearls.
sentences.n: al-luʾluʾ al-manthūr, “scattered pearls”, the commonest image for falling tears; the pearls are a collective singular.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ يَبْكِى بَكَتْ لِبُكَائِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathu Shamsu al-Nahāri yabkī bakat li-bukāʾihi
sentences.l: And when Shams al-Nahār saw-him weeping, she-wept for his-weeping.
sentences.i: When Shams al-Nahār saw him weeping she wept at his tears.
sentences.n: The print writes the final yāʾ of yabkī as ى, its usual habit.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ وَاللَّهِ إِنِّي عَجِبْتُ مِنْ أَمْرِكُمَا وَاحْتَرْتُ فِي شَأْنِكُمَا فَإِنَّ حَالَكُمَا عَجِيبٌ وَأَمْرَكُمَا غَرِيبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Abū al-Ḥasani wa-Allāhi innī ʿajibtu min amrikumā wa-iḥtartu fī shaʾnikumā fa-inna ḥālakumā ʿajībun wa-amrakumā gharībun
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said: By God, I have-marvelled at your-two's affair and become-perplexed in your-two's case, for your-two's state (is) wondrous and your-two's affair strange.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said, “By God, I am amazed at the two of you and bewildered by your case: your state is a wonder and your story a strange one.
sentences.n: The dual pronoun -kumā, “you two”, runs through his speech. Rhyme: ʿajīb / gharīb. The print writes shaʾn without its hamza (شان).

sentences.t: هَذَا الْبُكَاءُ وَأَنْتُمَا مُجْتَمِعَانِ فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ الْحَالُ بَعْدَ انْفِصَالِكُمَا وَتَفَرُّقِكُمَا
sentences.tr: hādhā al-bukāʾu wa-antumā mujtamiʿāni fa-kayfa yakūnu al-ḥālu baʿda infiṣālikumā wa-tafarruqikumā
sentences.l: This (is) the weeping while you-two (are) together; then how will-be the state after your-two's separating and your-two's parting?
sentences.i: All this weeping while you are together! What will it be like once you are separated and parted?
sentences.n: wa-antumā mujtamiʿāni is a circumstantial clause, “while you two are together”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ هَذَا لَيْسَ وَقْتَ حُزْنٍ وَبُكَاءٍ بَلْ هَذَا وَقْتُ اجْتِمَاعٍ وَمَسَرَّةٍ فَانْشَرِحَا وَانْبَسِطَا وَلَا تَبْكِيَا
sentences.tr: thumma qāla hādhā laysa waqta ḥuznin wa-bukāʾin bal hādhā waqtu ijtimāʿin wa-masarratin fa-inshariḥā wa-inbasiṭā wa-lā tabkiyā
sentences.l: Then he said: This is-not a time of grief and weeping; rather this (is) a time of meeting and gladness, so be-you-two-open-hearted and be-you-two-at-ease and do-not-you-two weep.
sentences.i: Then he said, “This is no time for grief and tears; this is a time for meeting and for joy. Be glad and cheerful, and do not weep.”
sentences.n: inshiraḥ, “expansion (of the breast)”, and inbisāṭ, “being spread out”, are both words for cheerfulness; here dual imperatives, addressed to the two lovers.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ أَشَارَتْ إِلَى جَارِيَةٍ فَقَامَتْ وَعَادَتْ وَمَعَهَا وَصَائِفُ حَامِلَاتٌ مَائِدَةً مِنْ صُحُونِ الْفِضَّةِ وَفِيهَا مِنْ أَنْوَاعِ الطَّعَامِ الْفَاخِرِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Shamsa al-Nahāri ashārat ilā jāriyatin fa-qāmat wa-ʿādat wa-maʿahā waṣāʾifu ḥāmilātun māʾidatan min ṣuḥūni al-fiḍḍati wa-fīhā min anwāʿi al-ṭaʿāmi al-fākhiri
sentences.l: Then Shams al-Nahār signed to a slave-girl, and she rose and returned, and with-her (were) maids carrying a table of dishes of the silver, and in-it of kinds of the food the splendid.
sentences.i: Then Shams al-Nahār made a sign to a slave-girl, who rose and went out and came back with young maids carrying a spread of silver dishes laden with every kind of rich food.
sentences.n: thumma inna …, “then (it was that) …”, a narrative opener. waṣāʾif, plural of waṣīfa, “young maidservant”. māʾida is the table, or the spread of food set out on it. min anwāʿ, “of the kinds”: min is partitive, “some of every kind”.

sentences.t: فَوَضَعْنَ الْمَائِدَةَ قُدَّامَهُمَا فَصَارَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ تَأْكُلُ وَتُطْعِمُ عَلِيَّ بْنَ بَكَّارٍ وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا يَأْكُلُونَ حَتَّى اكْتَفَوْا
sentences.tr: fa-waḍaʿna al-māʾidata quddāmahumā fa-ṣārat Shamsu al-Nahāri taʾkulu wa-tuṭʿimu ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin wa-lam yazālū yaʾkulūna ḥattā iktafaw
sentences.l: And they(f.)-set the table before-the-two, and Shams al-Nahār began eating and feeding ʿAlī son of Bakkār; and they did-not cease eating until they-had-enough.
sentences.i: They set the spread before the two of them, and Shams al-Nahār began to eat and to feed ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and they went on eating until they had had their fill.
sentences.n: ṣāra + imperfect, “began to, set about”. aṭʿama, form IV, “give to eat, feed”: she puts food into his mouth with her own hand, a lover's gesture.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رُفِعَتِ الْمَائِدَةُ وَغَسَلُوا أَيْدِيَهُمْ وَجَاءَتْهُمُ الْمَبَاخِرُ بِأَنْوَاعِ الْبَخُورِ مِنَ الْعُودِ وَالْعَنْبَرِ وَالنَّدِّ وَجَاءَتْهُمُ الْقَمَاقِمُ بِمَاءِ الْوَرْدِ فَتَطَيَّبُوا وَتَبَخَّرُوا
sentences.tr: thumma rufiʿati al-māʾidatu wa-ghasalū aydiyahum wa-jāʾathumu al-mabākhiru bi-anwāʿi al-bakhūri mina al-ʿūdi wa-al-ʿanbari wa-al-naddi wa-jāʾathumu al-qamāqimu bi-māʾi al-wardi fa-taṭayyabū wa-tabakhkharū
sentences.l: Then the table was-lifted, and they washed their-hands; and there-came-to-them the censers with kinds of the incense, of the aloes-wood and the ambergris and the nadd; and there-came-to-them the flasks with water of the rose; and they perfumed-themselves and fumigated-themselves.
sentences.i: Then the spread was cleared away and they washed their hands. Censers were brought to them with every kind of incense, aloes-wood, ambergris and nadd, and flasks of rose-water; and they scented themselves and stood in the smoke of the incense.
sentences.n: jāʾa bi-, “come with, bring”: the censers “came” bearing incense. ʿūd, aloes-wood; nadd, a compound incense of aloes-wood, ambergris and musk. qumqum (plural qamāqim), a narrow-necked flask for sprinkling rose-water. tabakhkhara, form V, “perfume oneself with incense smoke”.

sentences.t: وَقُدِّمَتْ لَهُمْ أَطْبَاقٌ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ الْمَنْقُوشِ فِيهَا مِنْ أَنْوَاعِ الشَّرَابِ وَالْفَوَاكِهِ وَالنُّقْلِ مَا تَشْتَهِى الْأَنْفُسُ وَتَلَذُّ الْأَعْيُنُ
sentences.tr: wa-quddimat lahum aṭbāqun mina al-dhahabi al-manqūshi fīhā min anwāʿi al-sharābi wa-al-fawākihi wa-al-nuqli mā tashtahī al-anfusu wa-taladhdhu al-aʿyunu
sentences.l: And there-were-set-before them trays of the gold the engraved, in-them of kinds of the drink and the fruits and the dessert-nuts what the souls desire and the eyes delight-in.
sentences.i: Trays of chased gold were set before them, holding every kind of drink, fruit and sweetmeat that the soul could desire or the eye delight in.
sentences.n: mā tashtahī al-anfus wa-taladhdhu al-aʿyun echoes the Qurʾān's description of Paradise (43:71). nuql, dried fruits, nuts and sweetmeats taken with wine. The print writes the final yāʾ of tashtahī as ى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَاءَتْ لَهُمْ بِطَشْتٍ مِنَ الْعَقِيقِ مَلْآنَ مِنَ الْمُدَامِ
sentences.tr: thumma jāʾat lahum bi-ṭashtin mina al-ʿaqīqi malʾāna mina al-mudāmi
sentences.l: Then she-came for-them with a basin of the carnelian, full of the wine.
sentences.i: Then a basin of carnelian full of wine was brought to them.
sentences.n: jāʾat … bi-, “she came with”, i.e. brought; who “she” is, Shams al-Nahār or one of her maids, the text does not say. ṭasht, a basin (a Persian word); ʿaqīq, carnelian or agate; mudām, wine, literally “what is kept long (in the jar)”. malʾān, “full”, takes no nunation.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اخْتَارَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ عَشْرَةَ وَصَائِفَ أَوْقَفَتْهُمْ عِنْدَهُمْ وَعَشْرَ جَوَارٍ مِنَ الْمُغَنِّيَاتِ وَصَرَفَتْ بَاقِي الْجَوَارِي إِلَى أَمَاكِنِهِنَّ
sentences.tr: thumma ikhtārat Shamsu al-Nahāri ʿasharata waṣāʾifa awqafathum ʿindahum wa-ʿashra jawārin mina al-mughanniyāti wa-ṣarafat bāqī al-jawārī ilā amākinihinna
sentences.l: Then Shams al-Nahār chose ten maids, she-stationed-them beside-them, and ten slave-girls of the singing-women, and dismissed the rest of the slave-girls to their(f.)-places.
sentences.i: Then Shams al-Nahār chose ten maids to stay in attendance on them, and ten slave-girls from among the singers, and sent the rest of the slave-girls away to their quarters.
sentences.n: Two Middle Arabic features: ʿashara with the tāʾ before a feminine noun (Classical ʿashr waṣāʾif, as the text itself then writes ʿashr jawārin), and the masculine pronoun -hum for the maids in awqafathum. Both are kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَتْ بَعْضَ الْحَاضِرِينَ مِنَ الْجَوَارِي أَنْ يَضْرِبْنَ بِالْعِيدَانِ فَفَعَلْنَ مَا أَمَرَتْ بِهِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ وَاحِدَةٌ مِنْهُنَّ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-amarat baʿḍa al-ḥāḍirīna mina al-jawārī an yaḍribna bi-al-ʿīdāni fa-faʿalna mā amarat bihi wa-anshadat wāḥidatun minhunna taqūlu
sentences.l: And she commanded some of the present-ones of the slave-girls that they(f.) strike on the lutes; and they(f.)-did what she-commanded of-it, and one of-them(f.) recited, saying:
sentences.i: She ordered some of the slave-girls in attendance to play the lute; they did as she ordered, and one of them sang:
sentences.n: ḍaraba bi-al-ʿūd, “strike with the lute”, is to play it; ʿīdān is the plural of ʿūd. amara bi-, “order (something)”: mā amarat bihi, “what she ordered”. al-ḥāḍirīn, “those present”, is masculine though it means the slave-girls, another Middle Arabic touch.

sentences.t:
بِنَفْسِي مَنْ رَدَّ التَّحِيَّةَ ضَاحِكًا * فَجَدَّدَ بَعْدَ الْيَأْسِ فِى الْوَصْلِ مَطْمَعِي
لَقَدْ ابْرَزَتْ أَيْدِى الْغَرَامِ سَرَائِرِي * وَاَظْهَرْنَ لِلْعُذَّالِ مَا بَيْنَ اَضْلُعِي
وَحَالَتْ دُمُوعُ الْعَيْنِ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَهُ * كَأَنَّ دُمُوعَ الْعَيْنِ تَعْشَقُهُ مَعِي
sentences.tr:
bi-nafsī man radda al-taḥiyyata ḍāḥikan * fa-jaddada baʿda al-yaʾsi fī al-waṣli maṭmaʿī
laqad abrazat aydī al-gharāmi sarāʾirī * wa-aẓharna li-al-ʿudhdhāli mā bayna aḍluʿī
wa-ḥālat dumūʿu al-ʿayni baynī wa-baynahu * kaʾanna dumūʿa al-ʿayni taʿshaquhu maʿī
sentences.l:
With-my-soul (I ransom) who returned the greeting laughing * and renewed after the despair, in the union, my-hope.
Indeed the hands of the passion have-laid-bare my-secrets * and they-showed to the blamers what (is) between my-ribs.
And the tears of the eye came-between me and-him * as-if the tears of the eye love-him with-me.
sentences.i:
My life for the one who returned my greeting with a smile, and after despair renewed my hope of union.
The hands of passion have laid my secrets bare and shown the censurers what lies within my breast.
The tears of my eyes have come between him and me, as though my tears were in love with him as well.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. bi-nafsī, “with my soul (would I ransom)”, the lover's oath of devotion. In line 2 the print gives the alif of abrazat no hamza after the sukūn of laqad; the metre (ṭawīl) needs it read laqad abrazat. al-ʿudhdhāl, “the blamers”, the stock censurers of love poetry. The last line's conceit: his tears blur her sight of him, as if they were rivals who wanted him too.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ شِعْرِهَا قَامَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ وَمَلَأَتِ الْكَأْسَ وَشَرِبَتْهُ ثُمَّ مَلَأَتْهُ وَأَعْطَتْهُ لِعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min shiʿrihā qāmat Shamsu al-Nahāri wa-malaʾati al-kaʾsa wa-sharibathu thumma malaʾathu wa-aʿṭathu li-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: And when she-finished from her-verse, Shams al-Nahār rose and filled the cup and drank-it, then filled-it and gave-it to ʿAlī son of Bakkār.
sentences.i: When the singer had finished her verses, Shams al-Nahār rose, filled the cup and drank it off, then filled it again and gave it to ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.
sentences.n: kaʾs, “cup”, is usually feminine, but the pronoun here is masculine (-hu), as often in this text. aʿṭā li-, “give to”: Classical would say aʿṭathu ʿAliyyan; the li- marking the receiver is colloquial.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
